mainTopic: The case of a wife's vow 'if I do not bathe', whether oaths count as vows, and what counts as עינוי for vows and for יום הכיפורים
overview: The משנה listed vows a husband can cancel, including 'if I do not bathe' and 'if I do not adorn myself.' A simple reading of 'if I do not bathe' fails, because she could just bathe and nothing would be forbidden. רב יהודה first says she conditioned it on bathing in foul flax water. That answer does not work for adorning, because smearing on נפט is not adornment. So he explains that she joined a vow with an oath. רבינא asks why the משנה then says only 'vows.' רב אשי answers that we either add 'and oaths,' or that oaths are also called vows, as 'כנדרי רשעים' shows. Next the גמרא asks how רבנן can call not bathing עינוי when bathing on יום הכיפורים carries no כרת. רבא answers that עינוי means suffering felt right away for יום הכיפורים, but anything that leads to suffering for vows. Finally the גמרא begins to set רבי יוסי against himself, since he ranks a city's laundry above others' lives, and this continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: What is the case of 'if I do not bathe'?
steps.stepSummary: Now that 'if I bathe' is explained, the גמרא asks how to understand the משנה's second phrase, 'if I do not bathe.'
steps.simpleTranslation: You have explained 'if I bathe.' But 'if I do not bathe': what is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on from the case it already explained and asks for the exact case behind 'if I do not bathe.' This line sets up the next moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists both 'אם ארחץ' and 'אם לא ארחץ' as vows a husband can cancel. The first was explained earlier. The negative version is harder to picture, so the גמרא needs a concrete case.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What is the case?

phrases.english: You have explained "if I bathe."
"If I do not bathe": what is the case?

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁנֵּית ״אִם אֶרְחַץ״. ״אִם לֹא אֶרְחַץ״ הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the explained case 'if I bathe' to the unexplained 'if I do not bathe.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact wording of a vow that matches 'if I do not bathe' and that a husband would need to cancel.

steps.title: The simple reading needs no cancelling
steps.stepSummary: If she vowed that bathing is forbidden forever unless she bathes today, she can just bathe today. Why would the husband need to cancel anything?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say she said: 'Bathing shall be forbidden to me forever if I do not bathe today,' why does she need cancelling? Let her bathe!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the most obvious reading of 'if I do not bathe' and shows that it does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, the ban only starts if she fails to bathe today. She can easily avoid it by bathing today, so she never suffers. The husband's power of הפרה would be pointless here.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a reading that will be rejected)
The husband's cancelling of his wife's vow

phrases.english: If you say that she said:
"The benefit of bathing shall be forbidden to me forever
if I do not bathe today"
Why does she need cancelling?
Let her bathe!
phrases.notes: If she bathes today, the condition never happens and nothing becomes forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first reading for the question in step 1 and knocks it down.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of 'if I do not bathe' as a vow conditioned on not bathing today.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: She can avoid the ban by simply bathing, so there is no hardship and no reason for הפרה.

steps.title: רב יהודה: bathing in disgusting flax water
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that the condition was bathing in foul flax-soaking water. To avoid the ban she would have to make herself repulsive, so the husband can cancel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: She said, 'Bathing is forbidden to me forever if I do not bathe in flax-soaking water.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a case where she really is stuck: either she does something disgusting, or she loses bathing forever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem in step 2 was that she could easily escape the ban. Now escaping means bathing in smelly flax water, which spoils her appearance. Either way she suffers, so הפרה makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Water in which flax was soaked, which is foul-smelling

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: It is where she said:
"The benefit of bathing is forbidden to me forever
if I do not bathe in flax-soaking water."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from step 2 by changing the condition to something unpleasant.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The condition was simply bathing today, which is easy to do.
steps.terutzMaskana: The condition was bathing in foul water, so either option causes her hardship.

steps.title: The same reading fails for adorning
steps.stepSummary: If we read 'if I do not bathe' this way, we must read 'if I do not adorn myself' the same way, meaning adorning with filthy נפט. But that is dirt, not adornment.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the same way, what the משנה teaches, 'if I do not adorn myself,' would mean 'if I do not adorn myself with naphtha.' But that is filth!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה's answer by applying it to the parallel phrase in the משנה about adorning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה uses the same pattern for bathing and for adorning, so one explanation should fit both. For adorning, the matching 'disgusting' condition would be smearing on נפט. But smearing on נפט is dirtying yourself, and the word 'adorn' cannot describe it.

phrases.english: Similarly, what the משנה teaches, "if I do not adorn myself,"
would mean: if I do not adorn myself with naphtha.
That is filth!
phrases.notes: Smearing on naphtha makes a person dirty, so it can't be called 'adorning.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's answer from step 3.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The parallel phrase 'if I do not adorn myself' would need a disgusting condition, but a disgusting substance cannot be called adornment.

steps.title: רב יהודה's second answer: a vow combined with an oath
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that she made a vow (bathing forbidden forever if she bathes today) and also swore not to bathe today. The same applies to adorning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: She said, 'Bathing is forbidden to me forever if I bathe today, and I swear that I will not bathe.' Or: 'Adorning is forbidden to me forever if I adorn myself today, and I swear that I will not adorn myself.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a new case that works for both bathing and adorning: she combines a vow with an oath, so she is trapped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath forbids bathing today. If she breaks the oath and bathes, the vow makes bathing forbidden to her forever. The 'not bathe' language of the משנה comes from the oath, and it works for adorning without any disgusting condition.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't confuse this with step 2. There the ban started only if she did NOT bathe, so she could escape it easily. Here the ban starts if she DOES bathe, and the oath also forbids bathing today, so there is no easy way out.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Yehuda said: It is where she said:
phrases.notes: The name in square brackets comes from the corrected wording. This is רב יהודה's second answer.

phrases.english: "The benefit of bathing is forbidden to me forever
if I bathe today,
and I swear that I will not bathe,"
"The benefit of adorning is forbidden to me forever
if I adorn myself today,
and I swear that I will not adorn myself."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the flax-water answer, which step 4 rejected, with a new case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The negative condition had to involve something disgusting, which fails for adorning.
steps.terutzMaskana: The negative wording comes from an oath not to bathe or adorn, joined with a vow, which fits both cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: This case brings oaths into the משנה, which sets up רבינא's question in the next step.

steps.title: Then the משנה should say 'vows and oaths'
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי: if an oath is part of the case, the משנה should have opened with 'these are the vows and oaths,' not just 'vows.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: The משנה should have taught 'these are the vows and oaths!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the wording of the משנה in light of רב יהודה's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה opens 'אלו נדרים שהוא מפר', 'these are the vows he cancels.' If the case includes a שבועה, the opening seems incomplete, because it mentions only vows.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
This one, "these are the vows and oaths,"
is what the משנה should have taught!
phrases.notes: The משנה's opening words only say 'these are the vows.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the משנה's wording fits רב יהודה's vow-plus-oath case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opening words of the משנה, given רב יהודה's explanation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If oaths are involved, a heading that mentions only vows is incomplete.

steps.title: First answer: add 'and oaths' to the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers: indeed, read the משנה as 'these are the vows and oaths.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Teach it as 'these are the vows and oaths.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי accepts רבינא's point and simply adds 'and oaths' to the wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of defending the short wording, רב אשי says to learn the משנה with the extra word. That way, oaths are clearly part of what a husband can cancel.

phrases.english: He said to him: Teach it as:
"These are the vows and oaths."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא by adding words to the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's heading covers vows only.
steps.terutzMaskana: The heading should be learned as 'vows and oaths.'

steps.title: Second answer: oaths count as vows
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, there is no need to change the משנה, because the word 'vows' also includes oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: oaths are also vows.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a second answer that keeps the משנה's wording as it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the word נדרים is read broadly, as a general word that can include שבועות. Then 'these are the vows' already covers רב יהודה's case.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces a second answer)
Are the same as; count as

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Oaths are also included in vows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to רבינא's question, one that keeps the משנה's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Broadening the meaning of a term
steps.terutzHavaAmina: נדרים means only vows, not oaths.
steps.terutzMaskana: נדרים is a broad term that also includes oaths.

steps.title: Proof: 'like the vows of the wicked' includes an oath
steps.stepSummary: A משנה rules that someone who says 'like the vows of the wicked' has vowed נזירות, a קרבן, and a שבועה. So an oath is called a vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: 'Like the vows of the wicked' means he has vowed regarding a nazirite, an offering, and an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to prove that oaths are also called vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase in that משנה is 'vows of the wicked,' yet it includes a שבועה. This shows that the word נדר can cover an oath, which supports the second answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the vows of the wicked

steps.whatToRemember: The case 'if I do not bathe / adorn' is a vow joined with an oath. The משנה's heading 'vows' either needs 'and oaths' added, or 'vows' already includes oaths, as 'כנדרי רשעים' shows.

phrases.english: As we learned: "Like the vows of the wicked":
he has vowed regarding a nazirite, an offering, and an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support the second answer in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that oaths are included in the word 'vows.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה on נדרים 9a: 'כנדרי רשעים' covers נזיר, קרבן, and שבועה.

steps.title: If not bathing is affliction, why no כרת for bathing on יום הכיפורים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבנן really hold that not bathing is עינוי נפש. A ברייתא teaches that on יום הכיפורים, כרת applies only to eating, drinking and work, not to bathing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do רבנן really say that when she does not bathe, that counts as affliction of the soul? Here is a contradiction. A ברייתא says: even though all the afflictions of יום הכיפורים are forbidden, the punishment of כרת applies only to eating, drinking and doing work. If not bathing counts as affliction, then someone who bathes on יום הכיפורים has failed to afflict himself. He should get כרת!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבנן of our משנה. It uses a ברייתא about יום הכיפורים to show that bathing does not seem to count as real עינוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה gives כרת to anyone who does not afflict himself on יום הכיפורים. If skipping a bath were true עינוי, then bathing would mean failing to afflict yourself, and it would carry כרת. Since the ברייתא says it does not, it seems that not bathing is not עינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They contrasted it': the גמרא brings a source that seems to contradict what was just said
Affliction of the soul, the kind of vow a husband may cancel

steps.confusionAlert: Bathing is still forbidden on יום הכיפורים. The ברייתא only says it does not carry the punishment of כרת.

phrases.english: And do the Rabbis say:
phrases.notes: These are רבנן of our משנה, who count a vow about bathing as a vow of affliction.

phrases.english: bathing involves affliction of the soul
when she does not bathe?
And they raised a contradiction:
Although one is forbidden in all of them
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means all the afflictions of יום הכיפורים, bathing included.

phrases.english: one is not punished with karet
except for one who eats and drinks
and does work, only.
And if you say that when she does not bathe
there is affliction,
then on Yom Kippur, when one bathes,
he should be liable to karet!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the oath and vow wording question to the claim of רבנן that not bathing is affliction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of רבנן that not bathing is עינוי נפש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If not bathing were עינוי, bathing on יום הכיפורים should carry כרת. The ברייתא says it does not.

steps.title: עינוי means something different for יום הכיפורים and for vows
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that each פסוק has its own meaning of עינוי. On יום הכיפורים it means suffering you feel right away. With vows it means anything that will lead to suffering, and going without bathing over time does.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: you can tell from the context of each פסוק. About יום הכיפורים it says 'you shall afflict your souls'. That means something whose suffering you feel right now, and not bathing is not felt right away. About vows it says 'every vow and every binding oath to afflict the soul'. That means something that leads to suffering, and if she does not bathe, it does lead to suffering.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. He shows that the word עינוי has a different meaning in each of the two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For יום הכיפורים, עינוי means suffering that is felt the same day, like hunger. Skipping one bath is not felt that way, so bathing gets no כרת. For vows, עינוי includes anything that will cause suffering later, so a long-term vow not to bathe counts and the husband may cancel it.

keyTerms.meaning: From the context of the פסוק
Leads to affliction, sooner or later

steps.whatToRemember: The same word, עינוי, can mean different things in different פסוקים. For יום הכיפורים it is suffering felt right away. For vows it is anything that will eventually cause suffering.

phrases.english: Rava said: from the context of the verse.
Regarding Yom Kippur, where it is written:
'You shall afflict your souls'
it means a matter whose affliction one feels now.
With bathing, one does not feel the affliction now.
Regarding vows, where it is written:
'Every vow and every binding oath
to afflict the soul'
it means a matter that leads one to affliction,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי לָא רָחֲצָה אָתְיָא לִידֵי עִנּוּי.
phrases.english: and when she does not bathe, it does lead to affliction.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two meanings of one word by the context of each פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עינוי means the same thing for יום הכיפורים and for vows.
steps.terutzMaskana: On יום הכיפורים, עינוי is suffering felt right away. For vows, it includes anything that eventually leads to suffering, like a long time without bathing.

steps.title: רבי יוסי's ruling about a city's spring
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets רבי יוסי against himself. It quotes a ברייתא about who gets priority to a city's spring, where רבי יוסי says the city's own laundry comes before other people's lives.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא contrasted one statement of רבי יוסי with another. A ברייתא says: a spring belongs to the people of a city. If the water is needed for their lives and for others' lives, their lives come first. If it is needed for their animals and others' animals, their animals come first. If it is needed for their laundry and others' laundry, their laundry comes first. If it is needed for others' lives and their own laundry, others' lives come first. רבי יוסי says: their laundry comes first, even before others' lives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge, this time against רבי יוסי. It is quoting the ברייתא that will be used to build the contradiction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי יוסי says that vows about bathing are not vows of affliction. Here, though, he ranks laundry above other people's lives. That only makes sense if going without laundry causes real suffering. The גמרא will now spell out why this clashes with his view on bathing.

keyTerms.meaning: He set רבי יוסי against רבי יוסי: two statements of the same person that seem to contradict

phrases.english: And he contrasted Rabbi Yosei with Rabbi Yosei:
phrases.notes: The first רבי יוסי is from our משנה, who says bathing vows are not vows of affliction.

phrases.english: A spring belonging to the people of a city:
if needed for their lives and the lives of others,
their lives come before the lives of others.
Their animals and the animals of others:
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording, so the case reads in full.

phrases.english: their animals come before the animals of others.
Their laundry and the laundry of others:
their laundry comes before the laundry of others.
The lives of others and their own laundry:
the lives of others come before their laundry.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: כְּבִיסָתָן קוֹדֶמֶת לְחַיֵּי אֲחֵרִים.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: their laundry comes before the lives of others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from challenging רבנן to challenging רבי יוסי of our משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's view in our משנה that bathing vows are not vows of affliction
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the spring ברייתא, רבי יוסי treats lack of laundry as serious suffering, important enough to outrank others' lives.

steps.title: If laundry involves suffering, so should bathing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to spell out the contradiction. רבי יוסי holds that going without laundry causes suffering. The sentence continues on the next עמוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if about laundry רבי יוסי said that it involves suffering...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting to explain the contradiction it just set up. The sentence is unfinished here and is completed on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning starts from laundry. If רבי יוסי thinks dirty clothes cause real suffering, the obvious next step is that not bathing should cause suffering too. That would clash with his ruling in our משנה.

phrases.english: Now, if about laundry Rabbi Yosei said
that it involves suffering,

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא כְּבִיסָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי יֵשׁ בָּהּ צַעַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the reasoning out of the ברייתא quoted in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's view in our משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If going without laundry counts as suffering, going without bathing should count as well. The argument finishes on the next עמוד.
